issues.legal_issue: A state agricultural land ceiling law is not wholly beyond legislative competence merely because it covers land in areas that may later be designated as urban agglomerations, and it cannot govern land already within urban agglomerations covered by the parliamentary ceiling regime.
material_facts: The state enacted a law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings across the state.
State legislative resolutions had transferred to Parliament the subject of ceilings on urban immovable property and related matters.
The parliamentary law covered specified urban agglomerations and allowed other areas to be declared urban agglomerations by notification.
The state law had become operative before any later notification could bring an additional area within the parliamentary law.
issues.conclusion: The state law was not wholly invalid. It did not apply to land in the urban agglomerations already covered by the parliamentary law, but remained within the state legislature’s competence for other areas until they were designated as urban agglomerations; the parliamentary law would then govern land remaining there.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 252(1) and (2), resolutions by state legislatures surrender those legislatures’ power over the matter specified, leaving Parliament alone competent to legislate on it; the resolutions here concerned ceilings on urban immovable property and connected matters. The Court relied on Union of India v. V.V. Chaudhary for the effect of such resolutions. A possible future designation of an area as an urban agglomeration does not remove state legislative competence before that designation; the state law cannot operate in areas already covered by the parliamentary regime.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_state_agricu: Landholders challenged the constitutional validity of a state law imposing ceilings on agricultural holdings.
predicates.state_law_covers_agricultural_land_acros: The state law applied to agricultural land across the state.
predicates.parliamentary_ceiling_regime_covers_only: The parliamentary ceiling regime applied to specified urban areas and to other areas only after they were designated as urban agglomerations.

issues.definition: When a challenged state ceiling law covers land across a region but the parliamentary ceiling regime reaches only designated urban areas, the state law is inapplicable in those covered areas and remains valid elsewhere until further designation.

issues.legal_issue: Land held by a minor son who has separated from the family through partition is included in the family unit’s holdings for determining the applicable land ceiling.
material_facts: The state law defined a family unit to include minor sons without distinguishing between sons who remained undivided and sons who had separated through partition.
The law applied the ceiling to the aggregate land held by members of the family unit.
A partition before the statutory cutoff was not invalidated, but land obtained by a divided minor son remained held by him.
issues.conclusion: A divided minor son remained a member of the family unit, and land held by him, including land obtained on partition, had to be aggregated with the land of the other members for applying the ceiling.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of family unit included minor sons, whether divided or undivided, and the provision applying the ceiling to the aggregate holdings of family-unit members required their lands to be clubbed. This aggregation did not invalidate a partition: the divided minor son could own the land separately while the land was nevertheless counted for the family unit’s ceiling.

predicates.land_ceiling_determination: An authority is determining whether land held by a person or family unit exceeds a land ceiling.
predicates.minor_son_is_included_in_defined_family_: The applicable definition includes the minor son as a member of the family unit whether or not he has separated from the family.
predicates.minor_son_holds_land_separately_after_pa: The minor son holds land separately after a partition.

issues.definition: If a ceiling determination concerns a family unit that includes a minor son who holds land separately after partition, that land is counted with the family unit’s other holdings.

issues.legal_issue: The distinction between minor sons included in a family unit and major sons excluded from it does not invalidate a protected agrarian reform law on the ground of unequal treatment.
material_facts: Landholders challenged the definition of family unit because it included minor sons but excluded major sons.
The challenged law was an agrarian reform measure.
issues.conclusion: The equality challenge could not succeed because the agrarian reform law was protected against challenge for infraction of Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A protects qualifying agrarian reform legislation from challenge on the ground that it violates Article 14, among other specified constitutional rights. The Court relied on the discussion of the corresponding contention in the companion Haryana land ceiling judgment delivered by Tulzapurkar J.
